passages.happening:
Four situations are named. A person hears a public call for witnesses and keeps quiet about what he knows: “he shall bear the iniquity” (verse 1). A person touches something unclean, such as the carcass of an animal, without realizing it (verse 2). A person touches human uncleanness without realizing it (verse 3). A person swears a careless oath to do something, and later realizes what he has done (verse 4).

“If someone incurs guilt in one of these ways, he must confess the sin he has committed” (verse 5). He brings a female lamb or goat as a sin offering. “And the priest will make atonement for him concerning his sin” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 4 set out the sin offering by the rank of the person. This chapter keeps the same offering and turns to everyday cases.

The first is about silence. When a crime had no known witness, the victim or the court could call out a public curse on anyone who knew the facts and kept quiet. In the book of Judges a mother speaks such a curse over stolen silver, and the thief, her own son, owns up. Justice in a village depended on people telling what they had seen. So Leviticus treats staying silent as a sin. Knowing and saying nothing is not innocence.

The second and third cases are about uncleanness. Touching a dead animal was not a sin in itself; it made a person unclean for a time, and time and washing dealt with it (11:24-28). The wrong here is that the person did not know, or forgot, and so did nothing about it. He may have gone near holy things in that state.

The fourth is a rash oath: words spoken to God without thought.

Then the chapter adds something chapter 4 did not say. The person ‘must confess the sin he has committed’. He has to say what he did. The offering is not a way round admitting the wrong. It follows the admission. The Hebrew verb for ‘confess’ comes from a root that also means to praise or give thanks. Both are ways of saying something openly before God.
passages.later:
Proverbs describes the silent witness of verse 1: “A partner to a thief hates his own soul; he receives the oath, but does not testify” (Proverbs 29:24).

It also describes what verse 5 offers: “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

David wrote of what silence about his own sin did to him: “When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3).

John writes to Christians, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).
passages.asks: The law treats keeping quiet about a wrong you witnessed as a wrong of its own. Ask whether there is something you know that someone needs you to say. And ask whether there is something you have done that you have never put into words before God.

passages.t: For those who cannot afford a lamb
passages.happening:
“If, however, he cannot afford a lamb”, he may bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering (verse 7). The priest offers them. “In this way the priest will make atonement for him for the sin he has committed, and he will be forgiven” (verse 10).

“But if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two young pigeons, he may bring a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a sin offering” (verse 11). He puts no oil or frankincense on it. The priest burns a handful on the altar.

“In this way the priest will make atonement for him for any of these sins he has committed, and he will be forgiven” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Here is one of the kindest provisions in the book. The price of the offering comes down, step by step, to meet what a person has.

A lamb or a young goat was a large part of a poor family's wealth. Doves and pigeons were cheap. They could be caught wild or kept round the house. And for someone who could not manage even birds, a little flour would do: a tenth of an ephah, commonly reckoned at about two liters.

The flour has no oil and no frankincense on it. Those went with the grain offering of chapter 2, a gift of gladness. This is an offering for sin, and it is kept plain.

There is no blood in a handful of flour. But the priest burns it ‘atop the offerings made by fire’, on the altar where the blood offerings were made. The poorest person's offering was joined to the rest.

And at each level the same promise is given: ‘he will be forgiven’. Atonement was never meant to be the privilege of people with flocks. The person with a handful of flour went home with what the owner of a herd went home with.
passages.later:
When Mary and Joseph came to the temple after the birth of Jesus, they brought the offering of those who could not afford a lamb: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:24).

The letter to the Hebrews chooses its words with care when it sums up the law: “nearly everything must be purified with blood” (Hebrews 9:22). ‘Nearly’ leaves room for this offering of flour.

Jesus watched a poor widow give two small coins and said, “this poor widow has put in more than all the others” (Luke 21:3).
passages.asks: God set the cost of coming back to him at what each person could bring. Ask whether you have ever felt too poor, in money or in anything else, to come to God properly. And ask whether your church makes it as easy for a poor person to belong as for a rich one.

passages.happening:
The LORD speaks to Moses again. “If someone acts unfaithfully and sins unintentionally against any of the LORD’s holy things, he must bring his guilt offering to the LORD: an unblemished ram from the flock” (verse 15). He must also repay what he has harmed, “adding a fifth of its value to it and giving it to the priest” (verse 16). The priest makes atonement with the ram, “and he will be forgiven” (verse 16).

Then a second case. “If someone sins and violates any of the LORD’s commandments even though he was unaware, he is guilty” (verse 17). He too brings a ram, “and he will be forgiven” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
This is the last of the five offerings. Its Hebrew name is asham, a word that can mean guilt, the penalty owed for it, or the offering that repairs it. Many scholars call it the reparation offering, because it always goes with putting right a loss.

The ‘holy things’ were whatever belonged to God: the sacrifices, the priests' shares, tithes, firstfruits and gifts that had been promised. To use them as one's own, for instance by eating a priest's share or holding back a tithe, was a breach of trust against God himself. The Hebrew word for ‘acts unfaithfully’ is used elsewhere of unfaithfulness in marriage.

The remedy is concrete. The person repays the full value, adds a fifth, and brings a ram. Forgiveness in this offering does not skip over repayment. It comes through it.

The ram is valued in silver by ‘the sanctuary shekel’. A shekel was a weight of silver, not yet a coin. The sanctuary kept a standard weight, which guarded both the worshiper and the priest against false scales.
passages.later:
Isaiah uses this very word of the servant of the LORD who suffers for others: “when His soul is made a guilt offering, He will see His offspring” (Isaiah 53:10). The New Testament again and again sees Jesus in that servant.

Jesus said that he came “to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), and many scholars hear an echo of Isaiah's chapter there.

The prophet Malachi accused Israel of the wrong described in verse 15: “Will a man rob God? Yet you are robbing Me” (Malachi 3:8). And he names how: ‘In tithes and offerings.’
passages.hard:
How can someone be guilty of a sin he did not know about (verses 17-19)?

Modern readers tie guilt to intention, so guilt without knowledge can seem unjust. Leviticus works with a wider idea, closer to what the law calls liability. A wrong can be real and do real harm whether or not the person meant it or noticed it. A driver who backs into a neighbor's fence without noticing is still responsible once he learns of it.

Interpreters read these verses in two main ways. One takes them to describe real guilt: the person has in fact broken a command and must deal with it once he suspects it. The other, argued by Jacob Milgrom, reads the key verb as ‘feels guilty’. It describes someone whose conscience troubles him, though he cannot name any wrong. On that reading the offering meets a very human need. It gives an anxious person a way to put the matter before God and hear that he is forgiven.

On either reading the text takes hidden sin seriously, and it refuses to leave a person with no remedy.

If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). The note on 2 Corinthians 7:8-12 says more about guilt that will not lift. Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: In this offering, being sorry was not enough; what was taken had to be given back, with more added. Ask whom you have cost something, in money, time or good name, and never repaid. And ask what a fifth added would look like in that case.
